title: Machine learning algorithms for climate change integration in evaluation: A conceptual model and simulated case application in Africa
domain: DRR + Education: Climate adaptation, disaster risk reduction, development evaluation
abstract: Climate change increasingly shapes development outcomes, necessitating its integration into evaluation processes. In Africa, recurrent droughts, floods and temperature extremes disrupt progress across sectors. Conventional evaluation approaches rely on static indicators and linear analyses, constraining their capacity to capture climate variability or explain how environmental shocks affect programme performance.
objectives: This study seeks to develop and assess an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven evaluation framework that integrates climate indicators into development evaluation systems to enhance analytical precision, relevance and timeliness.
outcomes: Findings indicate that climate anomalies are associated with observable changes in school attendance and learning outcomes. The model demonstrates the utility of AI in identifying climate–development linkages and generating more timely insights than traditional methods.
challenges:
-Conventional evaluation approaches rely on static indicators and linear analyses;Conventional evaluation approaches rely on static indicators and linear analyses 
- Limited capacity to capture climate variability or explain how environmental shocks affect programme performance 
- Need for scalable technical models for climate-responsive evaluation

title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence For Climate Resilience And Sustainable Natural Resource Management In Kenya
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) holds significant potential in enhancing climate resilience and supporting sustainable natural resource management in East Africa. Sustainable natural resource management requires a longof resources in order to meet current needs without compromising future generations. This can be achieved through adoption of AI which has emerged as a transformative tool in addressing critical environmental related shocks intensify, AI technologies are providing rapid and accurate insights for monitoring environmental changes, forecasting risks and informing adaptive responses. This study sought to examine how leveraging AI for climate resilience aids sustainable natural resource management in Kenya. The study was guided by one objective; to examine how AI can support sustainable natural resource management. Socio Theory guided the study. The study is adopted a desk top /secondary data research design. The study relie existing data published between 2020 and 2025. The targeted secondary data was 188government reports, academic journals and records and development partner publications relevant to the study topic. The sample was filtered down and reports forming the sample size. Data in this study was purposefully sampled and by methodically reviewed journal and articles, the inclusion criteria being publication date between 2000 tainable natural resource management. Data collection included structured online searches, document screening, and extraction of key variables linked to AI adoption and sustainable natural resource management. Thematic content analysis was also used to categorize findings into themes and analyzed thematically based on the research objective. The study findings indicate that AI enhances natural resource management in Kenya system level through improved monitoring, yet faces significant barriers at the exosystem and macrosystem levels, including inadequate infrastructure, data scarcity, and limited local expertise among others. The study further found that these structural constraints threaten and undermine the potential of AI in promoting sustai natural resource management. The study concluded that successful AI integration requires moving beyond isolated technological applications to foster holistic, cross-sector collaborations and robust data governance. ion on laying emphasize on the need for strengthening policy ecosystems through localized, ethical data practices, increased investment, and capacity building to bridge the digital divide. As with these innovations, AI’s gthen long-term climate resilience and reshape environmental governance.
objectives: This study critically examined how AI can be strategically applied to strengthen climate resilience and promote sustainable natural resource management in Kenya.
outcomes: AI technologies including remote sensing, machine learning, predictive analytics, and geospatial system are significantly enhancing climate resilience and sustainable natural resource management in Kenya by improving environmental monitoring, forecasting, decision-making, and adaptive planning across agriculture, water, forestry, wildlife, and marine ecosystems. Guided by Ecological Systems Theory, the study demonstrates that AI strengthens interactions between communities, institutions, and policy systems, promoting more resilient, participatory, and evidence-based environmental governance.
challenges: Limited data availability, inadequate digital infrastructure, and skills shortages.

title: AI-Enabled Climate-Smart Agriculture for Smallholder Resilience in Sub -Saharan Africa: A Systematic Review
authors: Deyemi Olatunbosun , Emmanuel Oluwasegun ISMAILA b, Mariam Iyabo Adeoba c, Olaitan Ebenezer Oluwadare, Tope Joseph Arayombo, Adedamola Oladunni f, Oluwafunmilayo Esther Ajiferuke  and Manfred Obinwanne Igwenagu
abstract: Background: Smallholder farmers in Sub-Saharan Africa are highly vulnerable to climate change impacts, including droughts, floods, and pest outbreaks, which threaten yields, incomes, and food security. Climate-smart agriculture (CSA) aims to enhance productivity, adaptation/resilience, and mitigation, yet adoption remains limited due to resource constraints. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools come as a game-changer to make CSA more accessible and effective for farmers with small farms. Aim: This systematic review synthesises empirical evidence on AI-enabled CSA interventions and their impacts on smallholder resilience in Sub-Saharan Africa. Methods: PRISMA 2020 guidelines were followed, with searches on Scopus, Web of Science, CAB Abstracts, Google Scholar, and AGRICOLA for studies published between 2015 and 2025. Eligible records were those with evidence of AI applications linked to CSA practices and resilience outcomes in smallholders. After screening 1,301 records, nine studies/reports made it to the final inclusion and were assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Results were synthesised narratively. Results: The nine included sources (covering Kenya, Tanzania, Mali, Ethiopia, Malawi, Nigeria, and Ghana) describe four main AI intervention types: image-based pest/disease detection, advisory chatbots, precision resource management apps, and predictive modelling. These models have already been used by hundreds to tens of thousands of farmers. Reported impacts include yield increases (e.g., +0.9–1 t/ha for rice, up to 25% for wheat), income gains ($200–600/ha), reduced input waste, and improved adaptation to shocks. All interventions align strongly with CSA pillars, particularly productivity and adaptation, with mitigation benefits from efficiency gains. Conclusion: AI-enabled CSA shows that it can be transformative for enhancing smallholder resilience in Sub-Saharan Africa, delivering modest but meaningful short-term gains in yields, incomes, and climate adaptation. Effects are positive, although it depends on the context of application, constrained by digital barriers. Policymakers and developers should prioritise inclusive, mobile-based scaling. Further long-term, rigorous studies are essential to confirm durability and broaden geographic coverage.
objectives: To synthesize evidence on AI applications supporting climate-smart agriculture in Sub-Saharan Africa.
outcomes: AI-enabled CSA shows that it can be transformative for enhancing smallholder resilience in Sub-Saharan Africa, delivering modest but meaningful short-term gains in yields, incomes, and climate adaptation. Effects are positive, although it depends on the context of application, constrained by digital barriers. Policymakers and developers should prioritise inclusive, mobile-based scaling. Further long-term, rigorous studies are essential to confirm durability and broaden geographic coverage
challenges: High implementation costs, poor connectivity, and limited access to digital technologies

title: Functional-Structural Plant Models and Artificial Intelligence: A Strategic Lever for Adapting African Agriculture to Climate Change
authors: Beda Innocent Adji, Xiujuan Wang, Mengzhen Kang, Doffou Sélastique Akaffou, Véronique Letort, and Philippe de Reffye
abstract: African agriculture, the pillar of food security and the economy for millions of people, is on the front line when it comes to climate change. Rising temperatures, more frequent droughts and variable rainfall are threatening the yields of traditional food crops. Conventional agronomic approaches are proving inadequate in the face of this challenge. This article proposes a paradigm shift by positioning functional-structural plant models (FSPMs), coupled with artificial intelligence (AI) methods, as a strategic tool for accelerating the adaptation of African agricultural systems. We present an integrated methodological framework (FSPM-AI) that starts with the collection of high-precision agro-physiological data in the field and culminates in the creation of “digital twins” of plants (i.e., dynamic virtual replicas of real plants). These models make it possible to simulate the complex interaction between a plant’s genetics, its 3D architecture, its physiology (particularly photosynthesis), and its environment. Using AI techniques for model calibration, sensitivity analysis, and simulation of future climate scenarios (e.g., representative concentration pathways 4.5/8.5), this approach makes it possible to (1) identify the key morpho-physiological traits that confer resilience (e.g., leaf angle, biomass allocation, and photosynthetic efficiency), (2) optimise cultivation practices (density and fertilisation), and (3) guide varietal selections. Using C4 cereals such as millet and sorghum, which are essential for arid areas but scientifically under-modelled, as an example, we illustrate how this coupling of modelling and AI can fill a critical knowledge gap and provide robust decision support tools for farmers, researchers, and policy makers in Africa.
objectives: The study aimed to develop and propose an integrated Functional-Structural Plant Model–Artificial Intelligence (FSPM-AI) framework to improve climate-resilient agriculture in Africa, particularly for drought-tolerant crops such as millet and sorghum
outcomes: The study found that integrating FSPMs with AI can create digital twins of crops, enabling researchers to simulate crop growth, assess resilience to drought and heat stress, identify key adaptive traits, and evaluate different climate and management scenarios before implementation in the field. The framework has significant potential to improve food security in Africa by supporting climate-smart crop breeding, optimizing agronomic practices, strengthening policy decision-making, and promoting the sustainable cultivation of resilient crops such as millet and sorghum
challenges: Data scarcity and limited technical capacity in agricultural systems

title: Fourth industrial revolution technologies for climate resilience in Africa: Integrating African indigenous knowledge for smart sustainability
abstract: As Africa confronts intensifying climate risks, emerging conversations around the Fourth Industrial Revolution and Indigenous Knowledge Systems offer promising pathways for resilience. While a handful of studies have explored and discussed this intersection, the conversations remain nascent and are marked by superficial consultations, limited co-design and a lack of clear metrics to assess community involvement or cultural relevance. This study contributes to this conversation, investigating how Fourth Industrial Revolution technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, Internet of Things, blockchain and remote sensing can be meaningfully integrated with African indigenous knowledge, particularly in climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, conservation and rural livelihoods.
objectives: To examine opportunities for integrating AI and indigenous knowledge in climate adaptation strategies.
outcomes: The study demonstrates that integrating AI, IoT, big data, and Indigenous Knowledge Systems can enhance climate resilience, improve drought forecasting, support climate-smart agriculture, and strengthen environmental governance in Africa. However, policy gaps, digital inequalities, infrastructure limitations, and insufficient recognition of indigenous knowledge remain major barriers to large-scale implementation.
challenges: Weak policy integration, digital divides, and infrastructure limitations.

title: Artificial Intelligence for a climate Just and resilient Africa
authors: Lyacoubi  Ayah, Bensiali Saloua, Minka Marcel  Loyd, Houedjiinnocent  Antoine,Boulaasal Hakim, El-Ayachi Moha
domain: Climate Justice, Climate Governance, Sustainable Development
abstract: In a time where global warming is making extreme weather events happen more often and with greater force, anthropic and natural risks have become a global menace  risking  the  livelihoods  of  most  vulnerable  regions  and  communities. This  challenge  presents  particularly  a  sever  threat  to  African  communities, especially those living in high-risk areas and ecologically fragile zones such as extremely  arid  zones  and  flood-prone  areas.  These  risks  are  results  of  many years of very extractive practices under the colonial rule; it is what is referred as “Colonial Legacies”
objectives: The purpose of this conference paper is to examine How colonial legacies have contributed to the climate injustice in Africa, and how digital innovations like AI can  be  harnessed  for  reparatory  justice  in  most  vulnerable  regions  to  climate impacts (e.g. floodplains, arid zones, informal urban settlements, etc.)
outcomes: Results indicate that there is a major gap in research about this topic. From the five selected papers, thirty-two contemporary climate risks in Africa, which can be  traced  back  to  the  colonial  era,  were  identified.  Existing  recommendations emphasize integrating customary knowledge with modern approaches, such as participatory  research,  legal  recognition  of  land  rights,  and  reintegration  of customary land and climate knowledge. While AI was not proposed as a solution, we proposed AI-based solutions with significant potential to advance reparatory justice  in  Africa.  AI  can  be  a  powerful  tool  provided  it  is  inclusive,  context-specific,    and    developed    with    active    participation    of    youth    and    local communities.
challenges: Risks include digital colonialism, unequal access to AI resources, weak governance frameworks, and the potential reinforcement of existing social inequalities.

title: Information technologies and artificial intelligence in climate-resilient agriculture in sub-Saharan Africa
authors: Violet P. Dudu; Masengo Ilunga; Dunisani T. Chabalala
abstract: The integration of information and communication technology (ICT) with artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative approach to improve climate change resilience in sub-Saharan Africa's agricultural sector. This bibliometric review analysed peer-reviewed literature on the evolving landscape of research on ICT and AI applications in addressing climate-related issues in agriculture in the region. Using VOSviewer software version 1.6.20, the analysis included metrics such as co-authorship analysis, keyword co-occurrence and citation analysis. For the period 2010-2025, the study shows trends, research clusters and gaps in using ICT and AI tools in agriculture, such as mobile advisory systems, remote sensing, machine learning and predictive analytics. The number of research publications remained low for the period 2010-2019, then rose steadily to a total of 26 by 2025. The findings revealed a growing focus on ICT-driven solutions for weather monitoring, precision agriculture and farmer decision-support systems, alongside AI's role in optimising resource use and forecasting climate impacts. Climate change was the dominant keyword closely linked to agriculture, food security, agricultural development, sustainable development, agricultural technology and ICT. South Africa had the highest number of co-authored publications (n = 8), followed by Kenya (n = 7). Challenges faced by farmers in adopting ICT and AI in climate resilience included lack of funding, inadequate knowledge, lack of technical skills and poor infrastructure. This review underscores the potential of ICT and AI to strengthen agricultural resilience in sub-Saharan Africa, while calling for more collaboration networks and partnerships to share knowledge and resources for ICT and AI development in agriculture.
objectives: To review how ICTs and AI technologies are being applied to support climate-resilient agricultural systems in Sub-Saharan Africa.
outcomes: As climate change continues to challenge agricultural practices in SSA, this study highlights the crucial role of ICT and AI as vital tools for enhancing climate resilience among smallholder farmers. Through bibliometric analysis, we identified significant trends that show how these technologies can promote sustainable farming. The study findings revealed that publications remained low for the period 2010-2019, then rose steadily until 2025. This shows an increasing interest in AI and ICT applications in agriculture research, as it is an emerging field, especially in SSA. Notable advancements in agricultural innovations include Esoko, implemented in Ghana to enhance overall farm management, and Nuru, an AI system that assists farmers in monitoring pests and diseases by offering guidance and recommendations based on the identified issues. Additionally, the FarmCrowdy platform in Nigeria is another digital solution that supports extension services to farmers, as well as the M-Kilimo mobile application in Tanzania. South Africa and Kenya have the highest number of publications on this research topic. South Africa and Nigeria have a strong collaboration, and the East African countries Kenya and Ethiopia also exhibit collaborations. The USA has collaborations with Kenya and Zimbabwe, demonstrating its interest in research activities in SSA. Our analysis reveals three key themes regarding how ICT and AI are being used in agriculture across SSA. First, the current ICT tools in use were identified, including widely used platforms such as WhatsApp and Facebook, mobile phones, computers, radio, the Internet, weather apps and specialised apps such as iCow and M-Farm in Kenya. These tools help farmers with crucial information related to their farming activities. Second, we highlighted the benefits and promises of ICT integration in agriculture and climate resilience. This technology not only improves productivity but also provides early warnings about climate risks and hazards, demonstrating its potential to enhance farmers' resilience to climate change. Third, we identified the barriers to the successful integration of these technologies. Challenges reported were lack of funding, inadequate knowledge, lack of technical skills and poor infrastructure. The analysis reveals that research publications, particularly in AI and its application in precision agriculture, are still lagging. Hence, there is a need for studies to focus on tailoring ICT and AI solutions to the specific needs of the smallholder farmers.
challenges: Major barriers include poor digital infrastructure, limited access to quality data, insufficient investment, skills shortages, and unequal access to AI technologies among farmers.

title: Computational Algorithms for Climate-Smart Agriculture in Sub-Saharan Africa
authors: Mulala Jamaima, Fredrick Kayusi , Timothy Mwewa , James Shabiti Mukombwe , Yusuf Umer, Petros Chavula
abstract: Climate-smart agriculture (CSA) provides a vital framework for enhancing food security, resilience, and mitigation in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), where agriculture is highly vulnerable to climate variability and shocks.  By  integrating  practices  that  sustainably  increase  productivity  and  reduce  greenhouse  gas emissions,  CSA  addresses  the  region’s  dual  challenges  of  climate  change  and  food  insecurity. Computational  algorithms  offer  critical  tools  for  supporting  CSA  through  simulation,  predictive analytics,  optimization,  and  decision-making.  However,  their  systematic  application  to  SSA’s agricultural  systems  remains  limited.  This  study  investigates  how  algorithm  development  and optimization can strengthen CSA adoption in SSA. The objectives are to examine the current status of CSA  practices  and  adoption  drivers,  explore  algorithmic  applications  in  modelling  and  resource management, identify integration barriers, and propose scalable pathways for sustainable deployment. A systematic review was conducted across six databases, focusing on literature published between 2010 and 2023. Screening yielded 32 eligible studies, which were synthesized through narrative and thematic analysis. Results highlight the use of algorithms such as particle swarm optimization, neural networks, and evolutionary computation in domains including yield prediction, drought risk assessment, irrigation scheduling, and crop disease detection. Key barriers include budgetary constraints, weak supply chains, policy  gaps,  and  low  farmer  awareness,  while  opportunities  lie  in  digital  connectivity,  climate information  services,  and  institutional  support.  The  findings  suggest  that  integrating  computational algorithms into CSA frameworks can enhance adaptive capacity, optimize resource use, and accelerate resilient food system transformations in SSA
objectives: The objectives are to examine the current status of CSA practices and adoption drivers, explore algorithmic applications in modelling and resource management, identify integration barriers, and propose scalable pathways for sustainable deployment.
outcomes: Results highlight the use of algorithms such as particle swarm optimization, neural networks, and evolutionary computation in domains including yield prediction, drought risk assessment, irrigation scheduling, and crop disease detection.The findings suggest that integrating computational algorithms into CSA frameworks can enhance adaptive capacity, optimize resource use, and accelerate resilient food system transformations in SSA.
challenges: Key barriers include budgetary constraints, weak supply chains, policy gaps, and low farmer awareness

title: Mediated influence of digital agriculture technologies on climate-smart agriculture decisions among smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa: a systematic review
abstract: Digital agricultural technologies like remote sensing, geographic information systems (GIS), artificial intelligence (AI), mobile-based advisory services, and the Internet of Things (IoT) potentially promise to enhance smallholder farmers’ climate-smart agriculture (CSA) adoption decisions in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). This study examines how digital technologies influence smallholder farmers’ decision-making regarding the adoption of climate-smart practices in SSA, focusing on identifying key technological pathways that enhance adaptive capacity and resilience to climate change. The study explored the role of digital agricultural tools in influencing CSA adoption. A critical analysis of 82 selected peer-reviewed articles published between 2015 and 2025 was conducted, identified through academic databases including Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. The review synthesized findings to identify consistent pathways through which digital tools support climate adaptation and agricultural resilience. Results indicate that digital technologies influence decision-making through three pathways: real-time information provision using IoT sensors and remote sensing, predictive analytics for climate risk assessment using artificial intelligence and machine learning, and optimized timing of farm operations through digital advisory and early warning systems. Empirical evidence shows improvements in resource use efficiency, yield stability, and climate risk preparedness using decision-support tools, although adoption remains constrained by barriers such as limited digital literacy, infrastructural challenges, affordability constraints, institutional capacity, social fabric limitations, and gender inequality. We conclude that digital technologies significantly enhance CSA adoption by reducing uncertainty and improving farm-level decision-making, although investment in infrastructure, digital literacy, and institutional support remains critical for scaling sustainable climate adaptation outcomes.
objectives: This study examines how digital technologies influence smallholder farmers’ decision-making regarding the adoption of climate-smart practices in SSA, focusing on identifying key technological pathways that enhance adaptive capacity and resilience to climate change.
outcomes: Results indicate that digital technologies influence decision-making through three pathways: real-time information provision using IoT sensors and remote sensing, predictive analytics for climate risk assessment using artificial intelligence and machine learning, and optimized timing of farm operations through digital advisory and early warning systems. Empirical evidence shows improvements in resource use efficiency, yield stability, and climate risk preparedness using decision-support tools.
challenges: Adoption remains constrained by barriers such as limited digital literacy, infrastructural challenges, affordability constraints, institutional capacity, social fabric limitations, and gender inequality

title: Innovations and policies for climate-resilient food and water systems in sub-Saharan Africa: a systematic review
authors: Unathi Kolanisi,  Denver Naidoo,  Lelethu Mdoda
domain: Water Resilience, Food Systems, Climate Adaptation
abstract: Sub-Saharan Africa’s food and water systems face increasing pressure from the worsening impacts of climate change, necessitating the integration of technological innovations and policy frameworks to build resilience. Despite increasing investments in adaptation, clear evidence on the combined impact of technological innovations and policy frameworks on resilience remains fragmented. This review fills this gap by combining empirical and policy-based evidence relating to the development of climate-resilient food and water systems across SSA. Using PRISMA 2020 as a guide, 7,548 records were retrieved, and 60 high-quality studies published from 2000 to 2025 were reviewed. Studies were analyzed using thematic coding in NVivo, based on CSA, IWRM, Vulnerability, and Climate-food-water nexus frameworks. Results show that climate-smart agriculture, improved irrigation, drought-tolerant varieties, agroecological practices, and digital advisory systems consistently enhance productivity and adaptive capacity, especially when implemented as integrated packages. However, effectiveness is constrained by limited financing, weak governance, fragmented institutions, inadequate extension systems, and inequitable access for women and smallholder farmers. Policy analyses reveal strong planning across NAPs and NDCs, yet significant implementation gaps persist, particularly at the local level. The review emphasizes the need for stronger institutional coordination, increased climate finance, and scaled multi-sectoral adaptation, alongside equity-centered and evidence-based approaches.
objectives: To evaluate existing innovations and policy approaches that improve resilience of food and water systems under climate
outcomes: Results show that climate-smart agriculture, improved irrigation, drought-tolerant varieties, agroecological practices, and digital advisory systems consistently enhance productivity and adaptive capacity, especially when implemented as integrated packages.The review emphasizes the need for stronger institutional coordination, increased climate finance, and scaled multi-sectoral adaptation, alongside equity-centered and evidence-based approaches.
challenges: effectiveness is constrained by limited financing, weak governance, fragmented institutions, inadequate extension systems, and inequitable access for women and smallholder farmers.

title: Advances in Artificial Intelligence for Climate Science: Methods, Applications and Evaluation Challenges
authors: Essam H. Houssein, Mahmoud Dirar, Abdelmaged A. Ali, Waleed M. Mohamed & Kadry Hamed
domain: Climate Modelling, Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR), Weather Forecasting, Energy Systems
abstract: Abstract Purpose To synthesize recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) (machine learning (ML)/deep learning (DL)) for climate science across climate modeling, extremeweather analysis, renewable-energy optimization, emissions monitoring, and climate adaptation. Methods Using a PRISMA-aligned protocol, we surveyed studies published between 2015 and 2025 across major scholarly databases. We extracted task definitions, datasets, model classes, evaluation metrics, baselines, validation design, uncertainty treatment, openness (code/data), and energy/CO2 reporting. Evidence is organized by application domain and by methodological rigor, emphasizing transferability and operational relevance. Results Strong evidence exists for improved short- to medium-range forecasting, nowcasting, bias correction, and anomaly detection. Physics-guided and hybrid models, including PINNs and neural operators, increasingly rival operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems in targeted settings. However, robust external validation, out-of-distribution testing, uncertainty quantification, and transparent reporting of code and computational footprint remain inconsistent. Conclusions AI enhances but does not replace physically based climate modeling. We contribute a field-level synthesis that combines PRISMA screening with a study-quality checklist to foreground evaluation rigor, reproducibility, and sustainability. Adoption of physics-guided architectures, probabilistic prediction, regime-aware validation, and carbon-aware benchmarking is essential for decision-grade climate AI.
objectives: To synthesize recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) (machine learning (ML)/deep learning (DL)) for climate science across climate modeling, extremeweather analysis, renewable-energy optimization, emissions monitoring, and climate adaptation.
outcomes: Strong evidence exists for improved short- to medium-range forecasting, nowcasting, bias correction, and anomaly detection. Physics-guided and hybrid models, including PINNs and neural operators, increasingly rival operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems in targeted settings. However, robust external validation, out-of-distribution testing, uncertainty quantification, and transparent reporting of code and computational footprint remain inconsistent
challenges: Challenges include model uncertainty, lack of high-quality datasets, explainability issues, and computational requirements.

title: A Systematic Review of the Economic Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Agricultural Productivity, Sustainability, and Rural Livelihoods
abstract: As agriculture confronts climate change, land degradation, labour scarcity, and food insecurity, the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a critical strategy to enhance productivity, sustainability, and rural resilience. This study explores how AI-powered digital agriculture transforms agricultural economics in developing contexts, with a particular focus on Sub-Saharan Africa. Using a structured literature review and thematic synthesis, we analyzed over 60 peer-reviewed articles and institutional reports published between 2020 and 2025. The analysis was organized around three key outcome areas: productivity, sustainability, and rural livelihoods. AI technologies, ranging from predictive analytics and advisory systems to smart irrigation, pest/disease detection, and precision fertilization, demonstrate a consistent pattern of impact. Studies reveal AI-driven yield increases between 12% and 45%, input cost reductions of up to 25%, and measurable improvements in supply chain efficiency. Furthermore, AI contributes to labour reallocation and market integration in rural areas. However, barriers such as infrastructure gaps, digital literacy, and policy vacuum limit scalable adoption. This review bridges technological applications with economic development frameworks, offering an interdisciplinary lens on AI’s role in agriculture. It articulates pathways through which AI enhances technical efficiency, environmental resilience, and rural economic transformation. This review is novel in its structured synthesis of economic outcomes using a triadic framework. It introduces comparative effect-size analysis to quantify AI’s impact in the study. The paper recommends investments in localized AI solutions, rural digital infrastructure, and policy environments that foster inclusive technology diffusion. The study contributes to the growing field of digital agricultural economics, providing evidence-based guidance for policymakers, agritech investors, and development stakeholders.
objectives: This study explores how AI-powered digital agriculture transforms agricultural economics in developing contexts, with a particular focus on Sub-Saharan Africa.
outcomes: AI technologies, ranging from predictive analytics and advisory systems to smart irrigation, pest/disease detection, and precision fertilization, demonstrate a consistent pattern of impact. Studies reveal AI-driven yield increases between 12% and 45%, input cost reductions of up to 25%, and measurable improvements in supply chain efficiency. It articulates pathways through which AI enhances technical efficiency, environmental resilience, and rural economic transformation. title: Harnessing GIS, Remote Sensing, and AI for Sustainable Land Use and Soil Resource Management in Africa
authors: Obasi Sunday Nathaniel, Chiamaka Obasi, Chike Onyeka Madueke, Nwosu Tochukwu Victor
domain: Land Degradation, Soil Health, Sustainable Agriculture
abstract: Sustainability  in  the  management  of  soil  and  land  resources  is  key  to  food  security,  environmental preservation,  and  development  of  Africa’s  economy.  African’s survival  has  faced  enormous  threats  and challenges such as land degradation, deforestation, desertification, and  the  impacts  of climate change over the  years.  There is  therefore the need  to find ways  to tackle these  situations using more  innovative and scalable ways.  This  review gathers information from current studies in the  use of Geographic  Information Systems (GIS), remote sensing (RS), and Artificial Intelligence (AI) for soil and land use management in Africa. A methodological systematic approach was used. This involves the screening of peer-reviewed publications, technical reports, and policy documents published between 2010 and 2025. The review basically looks at the dynamic  role  of  GIS  in  spatial  analysis  and  land  evaluation.  The  use  of  remote  sensing  in  vegetation monitoring and  soil dynamics  were  also looked  at.  The recent  AI adoption in predictive soil  map studies, degradation  modeling,  and  aerial  image  interpretation.  It  explores  the  synergistic  use  of  multi-source datasets and  hybrid approaches, alongside  institutional  and policy dimensions  such as open  data policies, capacity building, and public–private partnerships. Key points centered on the wide adoption and use of the emerging technologies such as drones, Internet of Things (IoTs), cloud computing, and big data analytics in precision agriculture and sustainable land management studies. There is however, huge set back emanating from data accessibility, technical expertise, and ethical guidelines for AI applications. The review concludes with  a  call  for increased  investment,  regional  collaboration,  and  policy support  to  fully  harness  digital technologies for sustainable soil and land use management in Africa.
objectives: To evaluate the contribution of AI-based geospatial technologies to sustainable land and soil resource management in Africa.
outcomes: The study found that GIS, remote sensing, and AI have significantly improved sustainable soil and land management in Africa by enhancing soil mapping, land-use monitoring, degradation assessment, and precision agriculture. The integration of these technologies with drones, IoT, cloud computing, and big data provides more accurate and efficient decision-making. The study recommends increased investment, capacity building, and stronger policies to maximize the potential of digital technologies in sustainable land managementies.

title: Monitoring African rangelands with remote sensing: Sensors, platforms, and the emerging role of machine learning
authors: Hooman Hosseini , Oliver Hensel , Abozar Nasirahmadi
domain: Rangeland Management, Biodiversity, Drought Monitoring, Ecosystem Resilience
abstract: African rangelands are ecologically and socio-economically significant ecosystems that require effective monitoring to support sustainable management. Remote sensing (RS) technologies, ranging from RGB, multispectral, and hyperspectral sensors to unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and satellites, offer valuable tools for observing rangeland dynamics. Various data analysis approaches, including traditional regression techniques and emerging machine learning (ML) methods, have been used to monitor rangelands, such as classifying vegetation, estimating biomass, assessing rangeland condition, and identifying grazing patterns. This review systematically explores existing studies that apply RS for monitoring African rangelands, organizing the literature based on monitoring objectives and highlighting commonly used sensors, platforms, and methods. While ML approaches, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), show potential, their adoption remains limited due to data scarcity and computational constraints. In addition, hyperspectral data, UAV-based monitoring, and high-resolution commercial imagery are also underutilized, largely due to cost and accessibility challenges. The review refers to emerging opportunities such as integrating Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and optical data, leveraging community-driven data collection, and combining UAV and satellite imagery. The paper concludes by outlining current challenges and pointing to potential directions for further research.
objectives: To review and synthesize the use of remote sensing technologies and analytical methods for effective monitoring and assessment of African rangeland ecosystems, with a particular focus on the role of machine learning compared with conventional approaches
outcomes: The review found that remote sensing is a valuable tool for monitoring African rangelands, particularly in vegetation mapping, biomass estimation, forage quality assessment, and grazing dynamics. The study revealed that optical satellite imagery remains the most commonly used data source, while advanced technologies such as machine learning techniques (including CNNs), hyperspectral imagery, UAVs, and high-resolution commercial satellite data are still limited due to challenges related to data availability, high costs, accessibility, and computational requirements. The review also identified promising opportunities for improving rangeland monitoring through the integration of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and optical imagery, the combination of UAV and satellite data, and the use of community-driven field data collection. Overall, the findings emphasize the need for increased adoption of advanced remote sensing and AI-based approaches, improved data accessibility, and further research to enhance sustainable management of African rangeland ecosystems.
challenges: The adoption of advanced remote sensing approaches in African rangelands is limited by scarce high-quality training datasets, high costs of hyperspectral and high-resolution imagery, limited access to UAV technologies, and inadequate computational infrastructure. The use of deep learning and SAR remains low despite their potential, while challenges such as limited ground-reference data, variable internet connectivity, and the complex, heterogeneous nature of African rangelands continue to constrain accurate monitoring and large-scale application of advanced RS techniques.

title: Closing Africa's Early Warning Gap: AI Weather Forecasting for Disaster Prevention
domain: Disaster Risk Reduction, early warning systems
abstract: In January 2026, torrential rains killed 200–300 people across Southern Africa and affected over 700,000, with South Africa declaring a national disaster on January 17. Despite meteorological agencies issuing warnings, the crisis exposed a critical reality: 60% of Africa's population lacks access to effective early warning systems [1], contributing to disaster death rates 4x higher than Europe and North America [2]. The structural barrier is cost – traditional radar infrastructure exceeds $1 million per station, limiting the continent to just 37 radar installations for 1.2 billion people, compared to 636 stations serving 1.1 billion in the US and EU combined. We present a production-grade architecture for deploying NVIDIA Earth-2 AI weather models at $1,430–$1,730/month for national-scale deployment enabling early warning coverage at 2,000–4,545× lower cost than traditional radar infrastructure while generating 15-day global atmospheric condition forecasts; periodic GPU forecasts are cached in PostgreSQL, enabling user-facing queries under 200 milliseconds without real-time inference. Our system, deployed in February 2026 to evaluate how Earth-2-based forecasting could be operationalized, demonstrates three technical contributions: (1) a ProcessPoolExecutor-based event loop isolation pattern that resolves aiobotocore session lifecycle conflicts in async Python applications, enabling reliable GFS data ingestion; (2) a database-backed forecast serving architecture where the GPU writes global forecasts directly to PostgreSQL and CPU servers query location-specific subsets in under 100 milliseconds, eliminating HTTP transfer bottlenecks for high-resolution atmospheric tensors; and (3) automated coordinate management pattern for multi-step inference across 61 timesteps, eliminating manual dimension tracking failures in production deployments. The system delivers forecasts through WhatsApp-based distribution architecture, reaching users through an 80%+ penetration communication channel. This architecture was deployed at national scale in South Africa. Countries with effective early warning systems experience disaster death rates 6x lower than those without. By reducing deployment costs from hundreds of millions to tens of thousands of dollars annually – achieving national-scale coverage at 2,000–4,545× lower cost than traditional radar infrastructure – this architecture enables continent-scale replication of early warning systems. UNDRR independently documents that such systems reduce disaster death rates 6x [4]. All architectural details and implementation patterns are documented inline to ensure full reproducibility.
objectives: To design and demonstrate a cost-effective, scalable AI-based early warning system using NVIDIA Earth-2 models that can deliver accurate national-scale weather forecasts and improve disaster preparedness in Africa at a fraction of the cost of traditional radar infrastructure.
outcomes: The study’s outcomes demonstrate that a production-grade AI-driven forecasting system can successfully generate and serve high-resolution, up to 15-day atmospheric predictions at national scale using NVIDIA Earth-2 models, significantly improving the speed and accessibility of early warning information. The architecture achieves substantial cost reduction compared to traditional radar-based systems, enabling national-scale deployment at a fraction of conventional infrastructure costs while maintaining operational reliability. It also shows that integrating GPU-based forecasting with a database-backed serving layer allows near real-time access to location-specific weather data, with query responses delivered in milliseconds, eliminating major computational and data transfer bottlenecks. In addition, the system improves dissemination of weather alerts through widely used communication platforms such as WhatsApp, enhancing reach to populations that lack access to formal warning systems.
challenges: Several challenges, including the need for sustained access to GPU and cloud computing resources, which may still be costly or difficult to maintain in low-resource settings. It also encounters complexities in large-scale meteorological data ingestion and processing, particularly with asynchronous workflows and system stability during real-time operations. Ensuring high forecast accuracy across diverse and rapidly changing climate conditions remains another key challenge. In addition, there are scalability issues related to handling large atmospheric datasets efficiently while maintaining low-latency access. Finally, limited digital infrastructure, connectivity gaps, and institutional reluctance to adopt AI-based forecasting systems may hinder full-scale implementation and integration into national early warning frameworks.
